item.title: Mangione lawyers say media limits at murder trial are unconstitutional, fear court will 'hand-pick' press
item.description: Luigi Mangione's attorney claims limiting his trial to 68 journalists and denying an overflow courtroom violates his constitutional right to a public trial
item.content:encoded:
Lawyers for accused UnitedHealthcare CEO assassin Luigi Mangione argued in a new court filing that the media access rules for his upcoming state murder trial violate his constitutional right to a public trial.

Karen Friedman Agnifilo, Mangione's attorney, argued in a Friday filing that limiting the trial to 68 journalists is unconstitutional, raising concerns that the court or district attorney could "hand-pick" which reporters are permitted to attend.

In the filing, Mangione's attorney raised three objections that they argue amount to a constitutional violation:

LUIGI MANGIONE'S FEDERAL TRIAL PUSHED TO NEXT YEAR IN ASSASSINATION OF UNITEDHEALTHCARE CEO

JUDGE REVEALS LUIGI MANGIONE WILL PURSUE PSYCHIATRIC DEFENSE IN UNITEDHEALTHCARE CEO ASSASSINATION CASE

Agnifilo claimed that her team wasn't consulted on media access for the upcoming September trial, and only became aware of a document titled "Media Access: PSNY v. Mangione" from an independent journalist on X.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"These guidelines were created without any consultation with or input from the defense. The guidelines provide that no overflow room will be made available for the duration of the trial, and that only six journalists will be permitted to cover jury selection, in a dramatic break from customary practice," she wrote.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Agnifilo called the process "unabashedly arbitrary and insufficient to satisfy the requirements of the Constitution."

Mangione's attorney is requesting a public hearing on the matter and wants the court to turn over a list of six journalists apparently picked to cover jury selection, the list of 68 journalists granted permission to cover the trial proceedings, as well as an explanation of the criteria and who made the selection.

Mangione's attorneys are also seeking details on what efforts were made to secure an overflow courtroom and are requesting that the proceedings be broadcast live, as there isn't currently an overflow room.

Mangione's federal trial won't begin until January.

Fox News Digital reached out to Agnifilo's office for comment.

item.title: Tony Romo's future with CBS is officially in question ahead of 2028 Super Bowl
item.description: J.J. Watt replaces Tony Romo on the CBS No. 1 NFL broadcast team alongside Jim Nantz and Tracy Wolfson as Romo's long-term future is unclear.
item.content:encoded:
CBS announced Friday that Tony Romo will be on leave until further notice, one week after he was arrested for operating a vehicle while intoxicated.

The network also announced that former Houston Texans defensive lineman J.J. Watt will replace Romo alongside play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson on CBS's No. 1 NFL broadcast team.

The fact that CBS included Watt in the announcement suggests it expects Romo's absence to extend into the regular season.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The development has naturally raised questions about Romo's long-term future with the network. But as OutKick has previously analyzed, those questions existed before his arrest.

CBS will televise its next Super Bowl on Feb. 13, 2028, following ESPN's broadcast this coming season. That game has long felt like the natural deadline for CBS to decide whether Romo remains its lead analyst.

For background, Romo signed a 10-year, $180 million contract in 2020. However, CBS is no longer the same company it was when he re-signed. CBS is now part of David Ellison's Paramount Skydance.

Ellison, the son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, has already reshaped CBS News since acquiring the company last year. Most notably, he installed Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief. He has made fewer changes on the sports side, though Paramount recently landed UFC rights in a reported seven-year, $7.7 billion deal.

The company paid such a premium for UFC that reports say the NFL wants to negotiate with Ellison before renewing its other television deals, believing he could reset the market with his willingness to overpay.

Put simply, Romo's contract would preclude most executives from demoting him from the Super Bowl with two years left on his current deal. The Ellisons are different. Larry Ellison is currently the world's sixth-richest person with an estimated net worth of $203 billion.

RYAN CLARK MADE IT TOO DIFFICULT FOR ESPN TO JUSTIFY KEEPING HIM AFTER YEARS OF CONTROVERSY

Again, questions about Romo's future existed before the OWI. Romo has become part of the story for the wrong reasons over the past three seasons. He frequently sounds unprepared, overly goofy and prone to forced banter with Jim Nantz that rarely enhances the broadcast.

The odd catchphrases, strained analogies, random noises and awkward jokes are well below the standard set by the other lead NFL analysts. The gap between Romo and Troy Aikman at ESPN, Tom Brady at Fox and Cris Collinsworth at NBC has become increasingly noticeable.

It's difficult to imagine someone as ambitious as Ellison wanting Romo to become a distraction during the first Super Bowl under his wing. And given the amount of coverage Romo generates during the season, he would almost certainly be one.

We suspect Ellison would still prefer that Romo show improvement this season and not have to remove the $18-million-a-year analyst from the network's top broadcast team. In theory, that path still exists. Yet it just became much steeper.

It's unclear when Romo will return, and now his OWI arrest and the viral video are also part of the story.

There's also a real possibility that J.J. Watt impresses both viewers and network executives. So far, Watt has shown promise as a color commentator. Put bluntly, he was better at the job than Romo was last season.

If Watt performs well to open the season and Romo returns only to continue struggling, CBS would have a difficult time putting Romo in the analyst chair for Super Bowl LXII next season, a decision that would have to be made before next September.

Think of it like a struggling starting quarterback who gets injured. If the backup plays better, history shows the better player often keeps the job, regardless of the guaranteed contract.

No matter what CBS says publicly in the meantime, Tony Romo's future is officially in question.

item.title: FBI releases eerie new age-progression renderings of accused University of Colorado student killer
item.description: New age-progression images show what FBI fugitive Thayne Alan Smika may look like now, 42 years after the Boulder murder of Sidney Lee Wells.
item.content:encoded:
More than four decades after a University of Colorado student was found shot to death inside his Boulder apartment, the FBI is asking for the public's help by releasing new age-progression images of the man accused of killing him.

Investigators on Thursday unveiled updated renderings of Thayne Alan Smika, who authorities said has spent decades evading arrest after the Aug. 1, 1983, killing of his former roommate Sidney Lee Wells, 22.

Police responded to an apartment complex in Boulder that day and found Wells lying on the living room floor with a gunshot wound to the head, according to the FBI. Wells was a senior at the University of Colorado Boulder studying journalism and was enrolled in the Navy ROTC program.

FUGITIVE TIED TO DECADES-OLD SLAYING OF PUNK ROCKER ROOMMATE CAUGHT IN TROPICAL HOT SPOT: FEDS

Smika, who was a 24-year-old student at the time, was identified as a suspect during the initial investigation but was not immediately charged. Three years later, in October 1986, authorities found his abandoned car in Beverly Hills, California, with a stolen license plate. He has remained on the run ever since.

A Boulder County judge issued a state warrant charging Smika with first-degree murder in December 2010. Days later, federal authorities charged him with unlawful flight to avoid prosecution and obtained a federal arrest warrant.

The FBI is offering a reward of up to $10,000 for information leading to Smika's arrest and conviction.

WOMAN ADDED TO FBI'S TEN MOST WANTED LIST ARRESTED HOURS LATER AFTER TIPS POURED IN FROM FLORIDA: PATEL

"It is never too late to hold a murder suspect accountable," FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski said. "The FBI is unwavering in our determination to deliver justice for victims' families. We will work with Boulder Police to pursue this fugitive until he is found and brought into custody to face the consequences of his actions."

Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn said investigators hope the newly released images generate fresh leads in the decades-old homicide investigation.

"We are hopeful these images generate actionable tips that our detectives can investigate to find Smika and bring justice in this case," Redfearn said. "No matter how much time has passed, we will never stop searching. We are grateful for our FBI partners for their help in creating these images and publicizing this crime."

Authorities said Smika would now be 67 years old. He may be clean-shaven or have a beard or mustache and may wear glasses. Investigators also said he does not have a valid U.S. passport and may have lived in Yelapa, Mexico, for years before 2007.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Boulder Police tip line at 303-441-1974, the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI or submit a tip online at tips.fbi.gov. Anonymous tips can also be made through Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at 720-913-7867.

item.title: 'Fire Country' star Diane Farr leaves Los Angeles after 30 years to start her 'third act'
item.description: Diane Farr shared an emotional Instagram video documenting her last day in Los Angeles after exactly 30 years, calling the move harder than expected.
item.content:encoded:
"Fire Country" star Diane Farr has left Los Angeles after 30 years.

The 56-year-old actress took to Instagram to share snippets from her "Last Day in LA," noting she has lived in the city for "exactly 30 years" and that "more importantly- I chose LA."

"I wasn’t born here, I didn’t go to school here - I just had a chance for representation as an actor and I moved out of NYC the summer I was 26," she wrote. "I came like most of the people I love in Hollywoodland - none of which I saw this week bc moving sucks."

She went on to say that she came to Los Angeles "chasing a dream that I am still shocked worked out."

‘SOPRANOS’ STAR JAMIE-LYNN SIGLER FLED HOLLYWOOD FOR TEXAS WHERE SHE NO LONGER FEELS ‘WATCHED’

Farr's acting career began in the '90s, with the actress landing her breakthrough role in "Roswell" in 1999. She later earned leading roles in "Numb3rs," "Splitting Up Together" and, most recently, "Fire Country."

In addition to her acting career, Farr also reflected on the many other positive experiences she had while living in Los Angeles, including starting a family.

"I also got to raise babies in the sun and the mountains and enjoy this beautiful home and attend public schools ??" she said. "Pinch me I’m overwhelmed by the blessings and hope, really hope I gave enough back. LA will always be where my family is from."

Farr shares three children with her ex-husband, Seung Yong Chung: son Beckett, 18, and twin daughters Coco and Sawyer, 17.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

The video showed snippets of her final day in the city, including shots of her saying goodbye to her home and her motorcycle, driving away in a 15' truck and photos of memories in the home.

She explained she has gone through many "phases" in the home and is now entering her "third act," in which she "settles into whatever it is I'm supposed to be...as a one," hinting it could include "a couple of countries I never saw myself in."

"We are just taking a hiatus now - a word I learned here - so we are letting the house go," she concluded her caption. "But god damn this was harder than I thought. To leave this house. To leave this dream, even if it is realized - and to leave home. Thank you #cityofangels."

Many fans took to the comments section to wish the actress good luck in the next chapter of her life, with one writing, "Good luck and safe travels as you start the next book in your series of life."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Another fan added, "Lots of great memories to remember ❤️ on the next chapter to make even more amazing memories ❤️," while a third wrote, "A new adventure awaits you, believe in the journey and the magic 🫶🏻💖🙌🏻."

The season four finale of "Fire Country" aired in May.

item.title: Weapons stockpile shortages impacting military strategy in the Mideast
item.description: U.S. missile interceptor stockpiles are shrinking, raising readiness concerns.
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon is confronting a growing reality after months of fighting Iran: America's stockpile of missile defense interceptors.

It is shrinking so much, military planners are weighing whether they can continue the current cycle of limited retaliatory strikes.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies, using open-source budget numbers provided to Congress, estimates U.S. Patriot interceptor inventories have fallen from roughly 2,300 pre-war to fewer than 827. 

THAAD interceptor inventories have also dropped from 452 to fewer than 278.

CSIS warns rebuilding those stockpiles could take three years or more, raising concerns about protecting U.S. forces and bases worldwide if another major conflict erupts, for instance in the Pacific.

"If you look at what we've expended for the Patriots, for example, over half the global inventory has now been consumed in the Middle East. Similar to the THAAD interceptors as well," said Kelly Grieco, a missile expert at the Stimson Center.

"These are things that we have to intercept ballistic missiles. Almost half of THAAD interceptors have been used. So that's global inventory. So that really leaves us with very little excess to be able to use in other theaters, whether it's defending US forces in Europe or the Indo-Pacific. So this becomes quite a constraint, I would say, on the United States capabilities, not just today, but in the years to come."

The Pentagon’s $67 billion request for fiscal year 2026 emergency funding includes $18.2 billion to replace the U.S.’s most advanced Patriot missile, Navy Tomahawks and the Army’s high-altitude interceptor known as THAAD, according to Bloomberg. 

Half of the munitions requested in the Pentagon's 2027 budget are low-cost munitions worth $600,000 or less. 

US NAVY PLANS MAJOR TORPEDO STOCKPILE OVERHAUL AS MILITARY SHIFTS TO TWO-WAR STRATEGY

By 2031, 70 percent of the munitions purchased by the Pentagon are expected to be in this lower-cost range, according to Jerry McGinn, who tracks the defense industrial base at CSIS.

"The munitions we use today are incredibly effective: the Tomahawk, the Patriot, the theater missile defense interceptors, or THAAD, that you've seen in the press are incredibly effective. They were built solely for performance, and they were designed a long time ago," McGinn said.

"They weren't built or designed to be produced at scale. So they take two to three years from this contract award to actually come off the assembly line because these are very intricate systems. They're essentially handmade in a lot of ways. So it's hard to scale production on these efforts."

Operation Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury burned through numerous missiles, but concerns about stockpiles preceded the latest Middle East conflict.

McGinn and others described a recent Pentagon meeting in which the department summoned a dozen leading Silicon Valley defense firms such as Shield AI and Anduril to discuss urgently replenishing depleted U.S. weapons inventories as the war consumes precision munitions.

"Concerns are that these companies have not produced at scale," McGinn added. "They have commercial kinds of technologies. They've done prototyping, but are they able to have production lines that can work with the government to produce those munitions at scale?"

Brandon Tseng attended the Pentagon meeting. 

This former Navy SEAL started SHIELD AI over a decade ago at a time when Silicon Valley did not want to partner with the Pentagon, and it was hard to get venture capital money. 

Just two years ago, 10,000 defense tech startups were formed.

"Defense tech was not a word in 2015. Venture capitalists thought we were crazy. When we said we wanted to work on this mission of protecting service members and civilians, they just didn't believe you could build a business behind it," Tseng told Fox. 

He was recently in Ukraine where his V-BAT, an AI-driven targeting system, is being used to strike Russian targets.

"It's a miniature Predator or Reaper drone. It does the mission of these $40 million aircraft at a fraction of the price — roughly a million dollars per aircraft," Tseng explained how Ukraine is using the cheaper version for "intelligence surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting" at very long ranges.

The V-BAT "can operate when GPS or communications are jammed because it has our AI pilot Hivemind on board," Tseng said.

TRUMP DECLARES HAMAS TO DISARM AS SAUDI MILITARY READIES FOR POTENTIAL HOUTHI GROUND OFFENSIVE

Ukraine is the battlefield where many of these tech start-ups are testing their weapons and adjusting their product "at the speed of war."

CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper developed an option for a 10- to 14-day intensive air campaign to cripple Iran's missile capabilities, according to the Wall Street Journal, reflecting concerns that the current tit-for-tat approach is becoming unsustainable as a result of dwindling numbers of these missile interceptors.

Iran's strategy is to target U.S. bases, forcing the U.S. to fire these exquisite defensive missile interceptors, forcing the Pentagon to take greater risks in defending U.S. troops the longer the conflict drags on. 

Iran believes that is its best hope at outlasting the U.S. military.

"This is clearly the Iranian strategy," Grieco said. "Every time they're firing missiles at U.S. bases, they're forcing the United States to intercept them, drawing down those stockpiles. And I think they fundamentally believe that U.S. interests are limited in this war, whereas Iran sees it as existential, and that ultimately the United States, if the IRGC continues driving up the costs, particularly human costs, will decide this is not worth continuing this fight."

item.title: Riley Gaines says WNBA is 'hellbent' on being an activist organization over a basketball league
item.description: Riley Gaines says the WNBA must choose between being a professional women's basketball league or an activist organization after Sophie Cunningham fallout.
item.content:encoded:
The reaction from some in the WNBA to Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham voicing her support of keeping biological men out of women's sports has been about what you might expect: wild.

With some wild behavior coming from the league, Riley Gaines gave her take on the matter in the latest episode of her podcast, "The Riley Gaines Show."

The former collegiate swimmer made it clear that she practices what she preaches and is focused on ensuring that women and girls get the opportunities in sports that were meant for them.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SEES SUPPORT SURGE AFTER STAR PUTS CAREER ON LINE FOR GIRLS SPORTS

"My entire brand has been built on protecting women’s sports," Gaines said. "And that’s not just a slogan that I say for social media or for clicks online. I really mean it. I want women to have the opportunity to compete and to succeed in their sport, whatever that sport may be.

"But the WNBA, they seem determined to sabotage (themselves) at every single opportunity."

And this time, as Gaines pointed out, this situation with how Cunningham and those who share similar views on the topic of keeping women's sports safe and fair — which is most people — has the league at a real crossroads.

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

"They can either be a professional women’s basketball league, or they can be an activist organization that occasionally plays basketball," she said. And it seems as if they’re hellbent on fulfilling the latter."

Of course, what is going on in the WNBA is just a part of the greater landscape. Gaines noted that the optics of adults — including a team owner — yelling at teenagers for supporting a common-sense belief is a disturbing look for society at large.

"When grown adults feel emboldened to pick on teenage girls, there is something seriously wrong with society," she said. "How could you possibly stand there and think that you are the bigger person?"

It's a fair question, and one that some folks are going to need to grapple with.

item.title: FIRST ON FOX: DHS points to ‘common sense’ reason for collapsing crime: ‘No surprise’
item.description: DHS links deportation of violent criminal illegal immigrants to collapsing crime rates, sharing details of gang members and convicts removed.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: As the White House touts "collapsing" violent crime rates in the U.S., the Department of Homeland Security is pointing to the deportation of violent criminal illegal immigrants as the "common sense" reason.

A new analysis by the Council on Criminal Justice (CCJ) released this month reported that homicides will "likely" reach a "new historic low" in the U.S. as most crime rates continue to decline mid-year. CCJ reported that homicides in a sample group of large U.S. cities are down 18% from the previous year, which is on pace for the lowest level since 1900. Additionally, carjackings are down 47%; motor vehicle thefts are down 20%; robberies are down 17% and residential burglaries are down 13%.

The White House touted the report as evidencing "extraordinary progress" in "delivering on one of President Trump’s core promises to restore law and order."

Assistant DHS Secretary Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital, "It is common sense. When you remove criminals from the country, crime rates fall."

ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF TRYING TO DISARM VIRGINIA POLICE OFFICER

The agency shared exclusively with Fox News Digital some of the "worst of the worst" criminal illegal immigrants who have been deported just in the last few weeks. Recent deportees include foreign nationals convicted of homicide, drug trafficking, aggravated assault, carjacking and other crimes, in addition to multiple with illegal re-entries into the country.

Among those deported was a member of the foreign terrorist organization Tren de Aragua, a Honduran national named Jared Adonay Cruz-Rivera, according to DHS. He was deported on July 18 following a previous conviction for robbery and an arrest on charges of drug possession.

DHS said that one deportee, Olegario Ramirez, a Mexican national and Paisas gang member, has a criminal history including convictions for homicide and illegal re-entry into the U.S. He was deported on July 27.

Another Mexican national deported the same day was Bulmaro Rendon-Ramos, a Surenos gang member, who had convictions for robbery, burglary and four counts of driving under the influence of liquor.

ICE ARRESTS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ILLINOIS TEACHER LINKED TO TREN DE ARAGUA MASS SHOOTING

Nammoun Khampanya, a Crips gang member from Laos, was deported on July 28 following convictions for cocaine possession, possession of a weapon, obstructing police and fraud.

A Cuban national, Omar Loaces Gonzalez, was deported on July 17. His criminal history includes convictions for vehicle theft and wire fraud.

Additionally, Haitian national Marc James Guerrier Pinard was deported on July 16 following his convictions for three counts of armed carjacking and an arrest on charges of burglary.

NEW YORK TIMES TORCHED FOR ‘FALSE’ REPORTING ON ICE INVESTIGATIONS, OUTLET FIRES BACK

Commenting on the deportations, Bis told Fox News Digital that "President Trump promised to make America safe again, and he has done just that."

"Crime has fallen to record lows under the Trump administration, including murders on pace to drop to the lowest level in 126 years. It’s no surprise that this drop in crime coincides with deportations of dangerous criminal illegal aliens," she said.

item.title: How much longer does Clemson head coach Dabo Swinney realistically have in Death Valley?
item.description: Dabo Swinney's job security at Clemson appears rock-solid despite recent struggles, but can Chad Morris and a talented 2026 roster deliver results?
item.content:encoded:
If I were to ask you to describe Clemson head coach Dabo Swinney in one word, your response would likely hinge almost entirely on how far back your memory goes when it comes to watching college football.

If you’re fairly new to the sport, you would probably use words like "washed" or "cooked" or even "fired" given his performance relative to expectations since the turn of the decade.

Fans who have been around for a while longer and know why those expectations exist at Clemson would opt to use words like "legend" or "champion."

'HOT SEAT RANKINGS' FOR ALL 16 SEC COACHES AS BEGINNING OF 2026 COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON DRAWS NEARER

However, if you’re an older college football fan and happen to remember the Tigers pre Dabo, you’d use words like "god" or "untouchable."

This is because you would be painfully aware of where Clemson was as a program in the years leading up to Swinney's arrival.

Sure, the Tigers have a national championship from the early 80s, but outside of that, no one was counting Clemson as a blue blood in the three decades before Dabo donned the tiger paw-crested polo.

CURT CIGNETTI REVEALS HOW WORKING FOR NICK SABAN CHANGED EVERYTHING: 'EVERY DAY WAS 4TH-AND-1'

From 1990-2008, the Tigers finished a season ranked inside the AP top-10 just once, as coaches like Tommy West and Tommy Bowden produced middling results year after year.

Enter Swinney, who, after becoming the full-time coach in 2009, has a robust 180-47 record, seven AP top-ten finishes, a remarkable nine ACC championships, and two national titles to his name.

All of that is to say, Dabo Swinney is Clemson football.

THREE INTRIGUING QUARTERBACK BATTLES TO WATCH DURING COLLEGE FOOTBALL OFFSEASON CAMPS

But after a disappointing 2025 season in which the Tigers went from top-five preseason Playoff darlings to Pinstripe Bowl losers, is the clock ticking for the winningest coach in ACC football history?

It's been well documented that Swinney is rather resistant to change in the world of college football, particularly when it comes to NIL and the transfer portal, both of which are seen as essential to competing in today's day and age.

You could make the argument that Dabo's unwillingness to embrace modernity has put Clemson a step behind the elites of college football, but the Tigers just won an ACC Championship and were in the College Football Playoff two years ago.

The question then becomes, is that good enough?

Is getting an invite to the dance but never being dangerous enough to win the whole thing acceptable now that Swinney himself has ratcheted up the expectations in western South Carolina?

That remains to be seen. The natives are restless, but as far as I (or anyone else, for that matter) can tell, leadership doesn't seem to be in a big rush to show Dabo the door.

That brings us to this coming season.

What will 2026 look like for the Tigers and what is a "safe" year for Swinney?

Contrary to what they showed last season, I think Clemson will have a big bounce back year this season.

As long as they get the quarterback decision right (and that's a big "if"), the Tigers have weapons like TJ Moore and Bryant Wesco Jr. to field a dynamic offense.

We talked about Swinney's affinity for familiarity in the face of change, so he will likely be thrilled to see an old friend in Chad Morris back on the headset as Clemson's offensive coordinator.

Morris was the OC for the Tigers from 2011-2014, which is right around the time the program started ascending, so maybe a familiar face from the glory days is just what Dabo needs to right the ship.

There is talent to be found all over this roster, but that's never been the issue.

I think Swinney and the Tigers will relish in the fact that no one is talking about them this offseason.

Leading up to the 2025 season, Clemson and Swinney were expected to compete for a national title, and they crumbled beneath the weight of their own goals.

This year's squad is similarly talented, but will be flying under the radar, and that could be a blessing.

The schedule is a mixed bag, though, as the Tigers open up with their fellow striped-cat brethren in LSU.

Outside of that game and a home contest against Miami, though, the slate for 2026 looks more than manageable.

Clemson will be the more talented team in almost all of their match ups, save for the two aforementioned games against LSU and Miami, so 9-3 or 10-2 is absolutely within reach.

That kind of year would easily buy Swinney some more time, but based on everything we've discussed, I'm not sure he even needs it.

Never say never, but I truly believe Dabo Swinney has the closest thing to a "lifetime contract" at Clemson that you'll see in modern sports.

Swinney has done everything he can to turn the Tigers into a traditional power in college football, so when the time comes for Dabo to call it quits, he will likely be doing so on his own schedule.

I don't know if Clemson will ever achieve the heights they reached in the 2010s with Swinney at the helm again.

For now, eight to ten wins and an occasional CFP berth might be the ceiling until Swinney decides to call it quits.

Or maybe the pendulum swings back the other direction with regard to NIL and the transfer portal, and Dabo looks like a genius playing the long game.

Either way, Dabo Swinney likely isn't going anywhere, this year or beyond.

Clemson fans will have to accept that and, in the meantime, appreciate everything the man has done for your program.

It will be a long time before another coach like him comes along.

item.title: The biggest threat in America's race with China isn't Beijing, tech executive warns
item.description: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar says power grid constraints and backlash against data centers threaten U.S. artificial intelligence progress more than China.
item.content:encoded:
America's biggest obstacle in the technology race with China may not be Beijing, but growing resistance to new data centers and the power needed to run them, according to Palantir's chief technology officer.

"The proximate issues are definitely going to be power and backlash against data centers," Shyam Sankar said in an interview with Fox News Digital at Palantir's American Builder Summit.

Sankar, whose company builds software for the Pentagon, intelligence agencies and major manufacturers, argued the U.S. risks slowing its own technological progress more than falling behind Beijing.

"The only threat to AI generating prosperity for America is suicide, not homicide."

LEADING ECONOMIST WARNS OF RISE OF 'GEN Z AFFORDABILITY SOCIALISM'

The U.S. and China are pouring billions into the race to dominate artificial intelligence, viewing the technology as central to economic growth, military power and geopolitical influence. Winning that race depends on an enormous buildout of data centers, power generation and transmission infrastructure to support increasingly capable systems. 

But those projects have drawn growing resistance from communities worried about electricity demand, water use and whether the benefits will outweigh the costs.

Companies have raced to build new data centers to support a wave of new computing infrastructure, fueling a nationwide expansion that also has sparked growing local opposition. The issue has spilled into the 2026 midterm campaigns, with candidates in battleground states such as Pennsylvania running ads focused on the economic and environmental effects of the projects.

Residents have raised concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, noise, traffic and whether utility customers will ultimately bear the cost of expanding the power grid. Some projects have been delayed or canceled, while lawmakers in several states have proposed restrictions or moratoriums on new facilities.

THE WAR ON DATA CENTERS JEOPARDIZES OUR ECONOMY AND NATIONAL SECURITY

Some developers have responded by pairing new data centers with dedicated power generation rather than relying entirely on the electric grid.

Sankar argues those debates risk slowing the industrial gains the technology can already deliver. He pointed to one submarine-parts manufacturer that cut production planning from two weeks to less than an hour, freeing enough capacity to add a third shift.

"There is no one on that shift who thinks, 'Hey, I got my job because of AI,' but that's actually what happened," he said.

The summit itself appeared designed to counter one of the AI industry's biggest public relations challenges: fears that technology will replace jobs. Rather than showcasing increasingly capable AI models, Palantir filled the stage with factory workers, healthcare workers and military personnel demonstrating software they had built to solve problems in their own workplaces.

Sankar argued the AI industry has become overly focused on pursuing artificial general intelligence, or AGI, rather than deploying today's AI systems across the economy.

Artificial general intelligence, or AGI, refers to a still-theoretical system capable of performing a broad range of intellectual tasks at or beyond human level, rather than excelling mainly at narrower tasks such as writing, coding or image analysis.

He compared the current moment to the early days of electricity, arguing that while technology already exists, businesses have yet to reorganize themselves around it.

"The AI we have is powerful enough that it should have created more prosperity and value," he said. "The only reason it hasn't yet is not a failing of the technology, it's a lack of our national will to push and invest in diffusing the technology through our economy."

"We shouldn't lose the plot in pining away for a machine god," he added.

The summit brought together a cohort of Palantir's American Tech Fellowship, where workers from industries including manufacturing, healthcare and defense demonstrated AI applications they had built for use in their jobs.

The demonstrations were intended to illustrate Sankar's contention: that AI will make workers more productive than ever rather than replace them.

That runs against much of the public sentiment, where workers across industries have begun to wonder how long until their jobs will be done by a machine.

"How many people have actually, at the front line, have experienced AI and how it's changed their job versus how many people are imbibing the fear-mongering from the social media feed, which is partially a Chinese psyop as well."

item.title: Planned Parenthood across Midwest at risk due to lack of federal funds after 3 facilities close in Michigan
item.description: Three facilities in Lansing, Livonia and Warren will permanently close after a $4.2 million drop in patient care reimbursements and federal grants.
item.content:encoded:
Planned Parenthood of Michigan (PPMI) announced Thursday that it is permanently closing three health centers across the state, pointing to a sharp decline in federal funding and Medicaid reimbursement restrictions pushed by national Republicans.

The organization will close facilities in Lansing, Livonia and Warren. None of the three locations provided procedural abortions.

"Republicans in Congress have now demonstrated that they are willing to block Medicaid reimbursement for Planned Parenthood patients, and the Trump administration has proposed eliminating the Title X family planning program altogether," Planned Parenthood of Michigan President and CEO Paula Thornton Greear said in a statement.

COALITION OF 25 STATES SUES TRUMP ADMIN OVER MEDICAID WORK RULE DESIGNED TO PREVENT FRAUD

According to the organization, the closures follow a $4.2 million drop in patient care reimbursements and federal family planning grants compared to the previous fiscal year. Additionally, the affiliate reported carrying an unsustainable $5.6 million in uncompensated and undercompensated care.

PPMI said the decision came after a comprehensive evaluation of its statewide network, following earlier cost-cutting measures that included eliminating administrative and non-clinical roles to prioritize direct patient care.

Planned Parenthood officials warned that reproductive health care providers across the Midwest face similar financial strains due to chronic underfunding, shifting state and federal Medicaid rules, and rising operational costs.

Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America’s Director of State Affairs Sue Liebel told Fox News Digital, "Michiganders deserve far better than Planned Parenthood for their hard-earned tax dollars. Not only is Planned Parenthood America’s biggest killer of babies in the womb, it is also known for botching procedures, killing or severely injuring women and girls in Michigan and nationwide."

"All three of the closed facilities exclusively sold dangerous abortion drugs, which are a more profitable method for the abortion industry, but have been found to inflict serious adverse effects like hemorrhage, infection and sepsis in as many as 11% of women who take them," Liebel added. "For every Planned Parenthood facility in Michigan, there are at least 20 community health centers offering women’s healthcare that are ready to welcome and truly serve low-income and other patients."

EXCLUSIVE: PENCE WARNS GOP 'MUST DELIVER,' OR PLANNED PARENTHOOD GETS TAXPAYER CASH ON FOURTH OF JULY DEADLINE

Thornton Greear signaled potential restructuring earlier this year after federal policy changes restricted Planned Parenthood’s Medicaid eligibility and Title X allocations.

"We have to reshape how we deliver care so Planned Parenthood of Michigan can continue serving patients for generations to come," Thornton Greear said. "That means concentrating our resources at regional access points and procedural sites and continuing to expand virtual care across Michigan. These are painful decisions, but they are strategic decisions grounded in where we can preserve access for the greatest number of patients."

The closures stem from federal legislation signed into law last year that restricts federal funds — including Medicaid reimbursements — from going to organizations that perform abortions. Under the provision, Medicaid reimbursements are barred for providers that receive more than $800,000 in Medicaid funds and offer certain abortion services.

EXCLUSIVE: PLANNED PARENTHOOD SET FOR MASSIVE TAXPAYER WINDFALL IF SENATE FAILS TO ACT

While federal law has long prohibited taxpayer dollars from directly funding abortion services in most cases under the Hyde Amendment, Planned Parenthood leaders argue the newer restrictions target their broader family planning and preventive health operations.

In February, Planned Parenthood voluntarily dismissed its lawsuit challenging the administration's Medicaid funding restriction. Despite the legal setback, organization leaders pledged to consolidate services into regional hubs and expand telehealth offerings statewide.

item.title: Navy SEAL and survival show host Joel Lambert warns Americans to prepare for weeks without supplies
item.description: Navy SEAL and survival show host Joel Lambert warns Americans to stockpile food, medications and water for a six-to-eight-week emergency scenario.
item.content:encoded:
Former Navy SEAL and Discovery Channel host Joel Lambert says Americans preparing for an emergency should forget the Hollywood fantasy of grabbing a backpack and disappearing into the wilderness.

Instead, they should start by making sure they can survive inside their own homes.

Lambert, author of "A Navy SEAL’s Bug-In Guide: How to Turn Your House into the Safest Place on Earth," joined OutKick’s "Tomi Lahren is Fearless" this week to discuss emergency preparedness, wilderness survival and what television survival shows get right — and wrong.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

While Lambert said he is optimistic about humanity’s future, he also warned that getting there could involve serious uncertainty.

"I think we’re heading toward a brave new world in a good way," Lambert said. "I think we’re in the fourth turning, and we’re moving into a golden age in the world and humanity. However, that’s going to be a bumpy ride."

That makes self-sufficiency especially important, he said, whether the disruption comes from war, political instability, a natural disaster or a widespread power outage.

Lambert’s advice is not built around one miracle tool or expensive piece of tactical gear. He said families should instead prepare for a scenario in which ordinary services and supplies are unavailable for an extended period.

"I think you need to be prepared for a, say, six-to-eight-week scenario where you’re not able to get prescriptions," Lambert said. "You’re not able to get medications. You’re not able to get grocery store runs, or they might be limited, or water issues or power issues."

That means having enough essentials to get every member of the household through several weeks without relying on a last-minute grocery run.

And sure, six to eight weeks of emergency supplies might sound a little alarmist — maybe borderline doomsday prep-y. But you don’t have to be staring down Armageddon or nuclear annihilation for those supplies to come in handy.

A hurricane, major snowstorm, flood or city-wide power outage can disrupt access to food, clean water, medication, electricity or cell service. These things happen all the time.

Lambert grouped human needs into five basic categories: shelter, water, food, communication and navigation.

"Shelter, water, food, which are the most important in that order, and then communications and navigation," he said.

Communication could include anything that allows a person to receive or transmit information, from a cell phone to a signal fire. Navigation means having the ability to travel safely and know where you are even when modern technology or infrastructure is unavailable.

The key, Lambert said, is to prepare before an emergency arrives.

"Get your house in order," he said. "Make sure that you have some food to get yourself through, you know, several weeks of uncertainty."

Lambert also offered a reality check for viewers who think watching survival television has prepared them for the real thing.

He described CBS’ "Survivor" as more of an elimination competition than a true survival program and acknowledged that even legitimate outdoor shows must make concessions for television production.

Lambert hosted Discovery’s "Lone Target," also released internationally as "Manhunt," which followed him as he attempted to evade military and law-enforcement tracking units in remote environments.

"When I started doing survival shows on Discovery Channel, I did not want to be a fake survival show," Lambert said. "I’m like, I just got out of the SEAL team. So I’m like, ‘if I’m going to do this, I’m gonna do it real.’"

Some high-risk portions, such as parachute jumps, were filmed separately so an injury would not derail an entire production. Lambert said the actual pursuits, however, were genuine.

"Everything that happened from the time I inserted ‘til the time I got extracted was real," he said.

He recalled an episode filmed in Africa in which he continued moving through an area where lions were hunting, despite the crew attempting to stop him.

Lambert said he encountered lions that had recently made a kill and realized he "could really literally die in the African bush doing the show."

Still, he continued.

"It’s better to finish and die than quit and live," Lambert said.

Spoken like a true Navy SEAL.

Fortunately, the average person is far more likely to face a power outage, storm or water disruption than a team of trackers and hungry lions.

For ordinary wilderness situations, Lambert recommended remembering the "rule of threes." A person can generally survive approximately three hours without shelter in harsh conditions, three days without water and three weeks without food.

That order matters.

"Everyone always tends to go to food immediately, just because that’s what we all think of, but you can go a long time without food," Lambert said.

Asked whether someone should drink directly from a creek or another natural water source, Lambert said the circumstances will always dictate the decision. But whenever possible, the water should be purified.

"In the wild, you always need to purify your water just ’cause you just don’t know," he said. "You can find the most beautiful mountain stream that’s just clear and perfect, and you don’t know a mile up there’s a dead buck or something laying in the middle of the stream."

WOULD THIS SURVIVAL POD MAKE YOU FEEL SAFER?

Lambert recommended carrying a portable filtration straw or hand pump, along with iodine or chlorine tablets. Those inexpensive tools can dramatically reduce the risk of becoming sick from contaminated water.

Fire is another versatile survival tool. Given a choice between hunting equipment, a tarp or a ferro rod in a tropical jungle, Lambert said he would likely choose the ability to make fire.

"Fire is shelter," he said. "It protects your corporeal body from the elements. You can purify water, you can cook food, you can signal with fire, you keep warm."

The lesson running through Lambert’s advice is that survival is rarely about possessing one flashy item or a singular strategy. The environment, weather and immediate threat should determine the next move.

But for most Americans, Lambert explained, the first move is much simpler. Build a reserve of food, clean water, necessary medication and basic emergency equipment before you need them.

Because when the alarms are already blaring, it may be too late to start getting the house in order.

item.title: Sophie Cunningham fan who was confronted by Storm co-owner opens up on incident and facing trans athletes
item.description: Ahnaleigh Wilson and her family speak out after Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton allegedly berated the teen at a WNBA game over girls' sports.
item.content:encoded:
Washington state high school athlete Ahnaleigh Wilson was pushed into a starting spot under the lights of the national culture war over women's sports this week when she was allegedly berated at a WNBA game.

Now, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, she and her family are speaking out for the first time since Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton was suspended for an exchange with the teenager.

Wilson went viral Tuesday night for speaking out about being allegedly heckled by Keaton during the Storm's game against the Indiana Fever. Wilson was not prepared to take on such public attention, and she and her family say it has caused them issues. The teen was there simply to support Sophie Cunningham after Cunningham took a public stand to save girls' sports.

"She was sitting directly across from us on the court, and we hadn't really noticed her much. And then she had walked over to talk to the people to the right of where we were sitting, and when she stopped talking to them, she turned and looked at us," Wilson, who sat courtside, told Fox News Digital.

STORM CO-OWNER SUSPENDED AFTER INCIDENT WITH SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FANS AS STAR BREAKS SILENCE ON CONTROVERSY

Keaton then allegedly called Wilson and her friend "f—ing insane," for her support of Cunningham and the protection of women's sports.

"After she was done, she kind of just walked away, and me and my friend were just like, 'What just happened?' Um, we were kind of stunned. I was like, "I'm not gonna cry, not gonna cry." Um, but I feel like I kind of cry, I don't know, when I feel overwhelmed or anything, honestly. So I started crying a little, and I was kind of embarrassed, 'cause I really didn't want to," Wilson added.

The emotional response was in part because of how personal the issue of protecting girls' sports is for Wilson. Washington is one of the 19 states in the U.S. that actively protects the rights of males to compete in girls' sports. So in eighth grade, she and her family said she lost a regional championship race to a biological male trans athlete in May 2024.

Wilson had to work her way back from a knee injury to compete in that race, and had the lead, up until the final lap, before the trans athlete zoomed past her and took first place. Wilson also said she had to compete against a male athlete four times this past school year in cross country.

"They don't know my story. They don't know that I've actually experienced this, and I've experienced it more than once. I'm going to junior year now, and I've competed against a biological male four times. these people don't even know what I've gone through," she said.

"It's disappointing, especially when it's other women."

So when Cunningham publicly took a stand for protecting girls' sports, it was enough to motivate Wilson to go to a WNBA game for the first time. She attended a rally outside Climate Pledge Arena in celebration of Cunningham.

But when Wilson got inside Climate Pledge Arena, she says she was heckled by other fans and eventually by Keaton, which brought her to tears, then spoke about the experience in a since-viral interview right after the game with independent Washington-based journalist Brandi Kruse.

When Wilson woke up the next morning, she slowly realized what she had gotten into.

Her friend opened Instagram first. One post about the incident appeared, followed by another. Then came coverage from national outlets. By the time the WNBA announced Keaton’s punishment, the story was everywhere.

"It was crazy," Wilson said. "I was expecting it, obviously, to kind of be big because it is a WNBA co-owner of the Seattle Storm and she was rude, but I guess I wasn’t expecting it to blow up that quick."

"It was pretty shocking. A little overwhelming, but also I was glad that the WNBA did something about it."

Her father, Brendan Wilson, said the family knew Ahnaleigh’s courtside sign might attract some attention. They expected a photograph of her supporting Cunningham to circulate. They did not anticipate their daughter becoming the face of a national WNBA controversy.

"She was going there with the intention of supporting Sophie and glad that somebody of Sophie’s stature was supporting Ahnaleigh," Brendan said. "She kind of expected her picture might be somewhere, that she was sitting courtside with a sign in support, but nothing of this magnitude at all."

The attention quickly spread beyond news reports about Keaton. Strangers found photographs of Wilson and began directing insults at the teenager and her family.

"Our daughter’s face is plastered everywhere," her mother, Elizabeth Wilson, said. "We are getting comments of hate. A lot of support, though, too, but this has exploded, and her actions have now impacted our family greatly and will continue to do so."

Wilson said she has tried to avoid reading the responses. The messages she has seen have accused her of being a bigot, transphobic and anti-trans. One commenter dismissed her as a "stupid white girl," she said.

"If you know me, you know I’m not any of those things and that I do care about people," Wilson said. "I’m okay with people being different and being different from me."

Wilson said her family has LGBTQ friends and relatives. She said her position is focused on the competitive consequences of allowing biological males into girls’ sports, not hostility toward transgender people.

"Those people don’t know me, and they don’t know that I love everyone," she said. "I don’t have an issue with people being trans. It’s just that it’s unfair when it comes to sports."

Elizabeth said the family has leaned on its Christian faith while trying to process the national attention.

"It’s overwhelming," she said. "We’re trying to continue to be Christ-like and trying not to be so angry and hateful. It’s definitely been a balance of trying to balance our feelings and just trying to let God lead us exactly where he needs us to go."

The Storm issued a public apology after the encounter became national news.

"We are aware one of our co-owners made comments to two fans in attendance at last night’s game," Storm majority owner Ginny Gilder said. "We apologize that this happened. Everyone who attends a Storm game deserves to feel welcome, and we remain committed to creating an inclusive environment where every fan is treated with respect."

The WNBA later confirmed to Fox News Digital that Keaton was fined and suspended from attending Seattle’s next five home games.

The Wilson family said it appreciated the speed of the league’s response but believes the Storm and Keaton still owe the girls a personal apology. They said no one from the team or the WNBA has reached out to them since the incident.

"They owe these girls an apology," Elizabeth said. "She needs to be held accountable. We teach our kids that every choice has a consequence, good or bad, and you have to own up to your mistakes."

Elizabeth also alleged Keaton’s actions made other spectators feel emboldened to target the teenagers.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM RALLY ROCKS WNBA GAME AS 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' ACTIVISTS FACE COUNTER-PROTEST

"By her coming up to them and verbally attacking them and bullying them into putting their signs away, she opened that up for the people around them to treat the other girls and our daughter and her friend in a similar manner," Elizabeth said. "She allowed that to happen."

The family also wants greater transparency about Keaton’s punishment.

"I’m glad that they took accountability, but five games and then they’re going to fine her, which is probably a drop in the hat, means, like, nothing," Elizabeth said. "We would just be interested to know: How much are they fining her? Where is that fine going?"

Brendan said he appreciates how quickly the league acted to suspend Keaton.

"I was glad that they didn’t waste much time in showing everybody that that kind of behavior is unacceptable and suspending her," he said. "This incident with our daughter, at least, was handled from the WNBA quickly, and we appreciate that."

But Elizabeth is still hoping for a personal outreach from the WNBA.

"We definitely would like to see them do something more personal, like reach out to our family personally and apologize for what happened," she said. "I think that’s a necessary step that hasn’t happened."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Storm for a response to the Wilson family’s statements.

The public attention was a burden for the family when it first began to pile up on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning. But their spirits improved as the day went on after the Storm apologized and news of Keaton's suspension came out.

But the most rewarding part came late on Wednesday night.

Ahnaleigh and her friend were playing pool when Elizabeth came downstairs and told them Cunningham had posted about them.

"We were all jumping up and down," Elizabeth said.

Cunningham wrote that she believed there was "a safe space and love for EVERYBODY," including biological girls and boys, transgender women and transgender men.

"Everyone is welcome at my table," Cunningham wrote. "You can disagree and still be kind. Bravo to those girls for standing up for what they believe."

Cunningham promised the teenagers gifts and called the conduct attributed to Keaton "truly embarrassing."

Wilson and her friend stopped playing pool and pulled up the post.

"We were shocked," Wilson said. "It was just insane. It was a super cool moment. It was cool to see her acknowledge us."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

The family said it would welcome the opportunity to attend another Fever game. It does not expect to return to a Storm game, even if Keaton or the organization eventually apologizes.

"We can’t support an organization like that," the family said.

"We would love to go see the Fever play again," Elizabeth added. "But I don’t think we’d go back to Seattle to watch them play."
